question: What is the main root cause of inherited degenerative diseases that affect the brain?

options.A: Traumatic head injuries from physical accidents
options.B: Acute bacterial infections of the central nervous system
options.C: Genetic mutations passed down through families
options.D: Severe nutritional deficiencies in early childhood

explanation: You've got this! These conditions happen because of faulty genes passed down in families, which slowly break down brain tissue over time. Simple and straightforward! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h1)

question: Why do inherited degenerative brain diseases often change a person's emotions as well as their body?

options.A: The genetic mutations directly damage brain areas controlling mood and personality
options.B: Brain cell loss only happens in areas that control muscle movement
options.C: Medications used for movement problems always cause severe anger
options.D: Patients simply feel sad because they know they have a chronic illness

explanation: Think of it this way: when the disease targets specific brain pathways, it affects both how the body moves and how emotions are regulated. Makes total sense when you picture it! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h1)

question: Which chemical messengers in the brain usually get thrown out of balance during neurodegeneration?

options.A: Blood proteins like albumin and globulin
options.C: Digestive enzymes like pepsin and amylase
options.D: Respiratory gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide

explanation: Spot on! When brain cells die off, it messes up neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin, which directly change mood, behavior, and thinking. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h2)

question: What causes sudden mood swings or impulsive behavior in patients with inherited brain degeneration?

options.A: A deliberate choice by the patient to worry their family members
options.B: An allergic reaction to routine hospital food and noisy wards
options.C: A temporary lack of vitamins due to poor daily eating habits
options.D: Damage to specific brain circuits that normally filter thoughts and impulses

explanation: Great job thinking through this. When the brain's physical filter systems break down, patients lose the ability to easily hold back sudden urges or emotions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h2)

question: Which mental health sign in degenerative brain disorders do families often mistake for sheer laziness?
explanation: You're doing great! Apathy means a deep lack of drive and emotion. Loved ones sometimes misunderstand this symptom as a patient just not trying hard enough. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h3)

question: A patient with a family history of brain degeneration starts accusing relatives of stealing items they just misplaced. What is this called?
explanation: Exactly. Developing false beliefs or paranoia means the person is losing touch with reality, which is a classic psychotic symptom of the disease. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h3)

question: Why is getting input from the family so crucial during a mental health assessment for these conditions?

options.A: Nurses are not allowed to speak directly with the affected patient
options.B: Patients may lack the insight to recognize their own behavioral changes
options.C: Patient memories always remain completely accurate throughout the illness
options.D: Family members are legally required to answer all diagnostic quizzes

explanation: Well reasoned! As the brain declines, patients often can't see their own mental changes, so family stories give nurses the true picture. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of doing regular mental health checks on these patients?

options.A: To prove that the family is doing a poor job at home
options.B: To test the patient's physical strength and walking balance
options.C: To find a permanent cure for the underlying genetic mutation
options.D: To catch subtle shifts in mood and thinking early and guide care

explanation: Spot on! Catching small mental changes early helps nurses update safety plans and support systems before things get overwhelming. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h4)

question: Which of these is a great non-drug way to handle behavioral symptoms in a patient?

options.A: Restricting all visits from family and close friends
options.B: Administering high doses of sedating antipsychotic drugs
options.C: Moving the patient to a completely unfamiliar location daily
options.D: Maintaining predictable daily routines in a calm environment

explanation: You got it! Calm settings and steady daily routines do wonders to soothe patients and lower anxiety without needing extra pills. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h5)

question: Why must nurses be extra careful when giving psychiatric drugs to patients with brain degeneration?

options.A: These drugs completely stop the physical progression of the genetic disease
options.B: Medications only work if they are given through an intravenous line
options.C: Their damaged brains make them more sensitive to side effects like excessive sedation
options.D: Patients with degenerative conditions are immune to all forms of chemical treatment

explanation: Brilliant. Because the central nervous system is altered, even small doses can cause strong side effects like heavy sleepiness. Always start low and go slow! [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h5)

question: What does 'anticipatory grief' mean for caregivers of patients with degenerative illnesses?

options.A: Grief felt in advance as they watch their loved one slowly decline
options.B: Anger at the medical team for failing to find a genetic cure
options.C: Relief that the patient's physical illness will soon be over
options.D: Confusion about how to fill out insurance and hospital forms

explanation: Spot on. Caregivers often mourn the gradual loss of their loved one's personality and skills long before the person actually passes away. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h6)

question: Why is providing respite care so important for family caregivers?

options.A: It cures the caregiver of any risk for developing the genetic disease
options.B: It teaches the patient how to live independently without any help
options.C: It permanently transfers all legal responsibility to the hospital staff
options.D: It gives them temporary relief from care duties to prevent complete burnout

explanation: You're doing fantastic! Respite care offers a much-needed breather so caregivers can rest, recharge, and protect their own health. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h6)

question: When is the best time to talk about advance directives with a patient diagnosed with a brain degenerative disease?

options.A: Family members should make all choices without consulting the patient
options.B: After the patient has completely lost the ability to speak or think
options.C: Early in the disease process while the patient can still make decisions
options.D: During an emergency room visit in the final week of life

explanation: Makes total sense! Talking early ensures the patient's own values guide their future care before cognitive decline takes away their voice. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h7)

question: What is the main ethical focus of nursing care during the final stages of a degenerative disease?

options.A: Preserving patient dignity and providing comfort
options.B: Limiting family visits to reduce hospital noise and confusion
options.C: Forcing the patient to eat regular meals against their will
options.D: Finding experimental genetic treatments to reverse brain damage

explanation: You nailed it! When a disease reaches its end stage, the goal shifts from stopping the decline to ensuring comfort, pain relief, and deep dignity. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T13#GNS222_U4_T13_h7)
